verdicts.reason: Both score whether a rule document cites its governing statutory/regulatory authority properly; the codification clause is a minor rider on the same authority-citation construct.
Both grade whether an NPRM/FR notice carries the APA- and FR-required content elements and publication details, differing only in which required elements they enumerate.

Both are omnibus 'comment quality/effectiveness' composites built from the same ingredients (specificity, evidence/data, engagement, concrete recommendations) and would rank comments nearly identically.
Both measure whether costs and benefits are broken out by who bears and who receives them, i.e. distributional analysis under two names.

X scores identification/targeting of the proceeding and sections, while Y scores evidentiary support and concrete change requests; a precisely targeted comment with no data scores high on X and low on Y.
Both measure whether PRA information collections are identified and their burden (respondents, frequency, hours, costs) reported transparently and completely.
Both are whole-document FR compliance checks over essentially the same required-element/metadata checklist (identifiers, authority citations, summary, contacts, format).
Identical concept restated: the commenter supplies its own numeric compliance-cost figure and states where the number came from.
Both measure whether the comment offers a concrete, adoptable alternative regulatory design rather than mere objection.
Both score whether the comment pinpoints the docket and the exact provisions it addresses; X's 'targeting and identification' and Y's 'pinpoint provisions and docket' name one property.

X centers on Title IX coverage/authority and access to sex-segregated programs and facilities, while Y centers on defining covered sex-based conduct and harassment; a document can do one thoroughly and not the other.
X is the narrow property of engaging the proposal text and record, while Y is a broad quality composite additionally demanding timeliness, traceable data, alternatives, and quantitative content.
X grades EJ impact assessment and analytic tooling (e.g. EJSCREEN), while Y grades community engagement and embedding EJ into permitting/program design and mitigation, which are separately scorable.
Both measure the completeness and transparency of PRA ICR burden estimates (respondents, frequency, time per response, total hours, associated costs).
X is environment-specific EJ assessment plus permitting/program design, while Y is general distributional/equity analysis across subgroups; scope and object of measurement differ.

X asks whether the SIP addresses the required elements and area programs, while Y asks whether it meets stringency, enforceability, and 110(l) approvability standards; a complete SIP can still fail approvability.

Y is the narrow property of authority citation and codification, while X grades the full FR metadata/structure package; a document with perfect authority lines can be missing dates, addresses, or signatures.
Both measure organization and readability of the comment (summary up front, headings/section-by-section structure, logical flow, usable presentation).
First-hand operational experience is a content/standing property; intensity of expressed approval is an affective property explicitly independent of evidence.
Both score identification of PRA-covered collections plus the standard burden breakdown and total-hours estimation quality.
Presence of CFR citations is a formal citation property; arguing the rule exceeds statutory authority is a substantive legal claim; either can appear without the other.
Y is confined to engagement with the RIA/economic analysis, while X is a broad comment-quality composite; a strong comment on other dimensions may never touch the RIA.

X scores responsiveness to the agency's enumerated questions specifically, while Y scores broader engagement with the regulatory text and analytic record, which a comment can do without answering the questions.
Both grade the adequacy of NEPA EIS process and documentation (scoping, alternatives, required content, supplemental review, decision documentation).
Both enumerate the same Title IX grievance-procedure compliance requirements (notice, evidence rules, hearings/cross-examination, informal resolution, training, recordkeeping).
Both require distributional consequences across affected subgroups to be made explicit; 'equity' is the normative framing of the same disaggregation.
Both measure transparency and authenticity of mass-comment campaigns (sponsor/coalition disclosure, astroturf/fake-comment handling, documented design and duplication signals).
X is confined to claims being checkable and cited, while Y additionally scores argument construction (structure, signal-to-noise, rebutting counterarguments), a separately scorable dimension.
Both measure whether assertions are backed by complete, verifiable, reliable citations; 'verifiable claims' and 'evidentiary reliability' name one property.
X measures the accuracy and methodology of burden estimation, while Y measures demonstrated efforts to minimize burden and solicit comment on reduction; a precise estimate need not show minimization.
Both measure interagency/cross-jurisdictional coordination and harmonization to avoid duplication and keep methods and requirements coherent.
Both grade whether the Federal Register document contains the required headings, sections, authority/signature blocks, and drafting/format conventions.
